source_text:
Σπουδάσωμεν οὖν, ἀγαπητοί, τὰς ἀρετὰς ταύτας μετελθεῖν, ἵνα

τῆς τῶν οὐρανῶν βασιλείας καταξιωθῶμεν. Μὴ ἴσθι, ἀγαπητέ, περὶ μὲν τὴν πίστιν
σπουδαῖος, περὶ δὲ τὴν σπουδὴν ὀκνηρότερος, μὴ περὶ μὲν τὰς γραφὰς φιλόπονος,
περὶ δὲ τὰ ἤθη ἀφιλόσοφος· πλουτεῖν γὰρ δεῖ ἐν ἔργοις ἀγαθοῖς, ἐν λόγῳ, ἐν σοφίᾳ,
ἐν σωφροσύνῃ, ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ, ἐν ἀνδρείᾳ, ἐν εὐσεβείᾳ, ἐν φρονήσει καὶ ὁσιότητι·
ὥσπερ γὰρ ἡ κακία καὶ πρὸ τῆς γεέννης κολάζει τοὺς μετιόντας αὐτήν, οὕτως ἡ
ἀρετὴ τοὺς ἐργαζομένους αὐτὴν καὶ πρὸ τῆς βασιλείας παρασκευάζει τρυφᾶν.

1
orientation: The preacher is closing his address to the congregation, urging them to pursue all the virtues he has just discussed so that they may be counted worthy of the kingdom of heaven.
pass_a_gloss: Let us be eager, then, beloved, [to] pursue these virtues, so that we may be counted worthy of the kingdom of heaven. Do not be, beloved, zealous concerning faith but more sluggish concerning zeal, nor hardworking concerning the scriptures but unphilosophical concerning character; for [one] must be rich in good works, in word, in wisdom, in self-control, in righteousness, in courage, in piety, in prudence and holiness; for just as wickedness even before Gehenna punishes those who pursue it, so virtue makes those who work it even before the kingdom to rejoice.

choices.why: The verb denotes earnest effort or zeal, matching the homily's repeated call to pursue virtue with zeal.
The verb means to go after or seek to attain, fitting the image of pursuing virtues as a goal.
The verb means to be deemed or judged worthy, preserving the passive sense of being granted worthiness by God.
The comparative of ὀκνηρός means more hesitant or lazy, contrasting with σπουδαῖος (zealous).
The word literally means without love of wisdom, contrasting with φιλόπονος (hardworking) and implying neglect of moral formation.
The verb means to live softly or luxuriously, conveying the joy and delight virtue brings even before the kingdom.

pass_b_english: So then, beloved, let us be eager to pursue these virtues, so that we may be counted worthy of the kingdom of heaven. Do not be zealous about faith, beloved, yet more sluggish about zeal itself; do not be hardworking about the Scriptures, yet unphilosophical about your character. For you must be rich in good works, in word, in wisdom, in self-control, in righteousness, in courage, in piety, in prudence, and in holiness. For just as wickedness punishes those who pursue it even before hell, so virtue makes those who work at it feast in delight even before the kingdom.

problems.why: τρυφᾶν here means 'rejoice/delight', not 'live in luxury' with negative connotation

edits.old: so virtue makes those who work at it live in luxury even before the kingdom.
edits.new: so virtue makes those who work at it rejoice even before the kingdom.

fixed: Changed 'live in luxury' to 'rejoice' in both the English and the literal gloss, since τρυφᾶν here means 'rejoice/delight' rather than 'live in luxury' with negative connotation.

problems.why: τρυφᾶν means 'live in luxury/delight', not 'rejoice'; the sense is feasting/enjoying delights, not merely being glad.
problems.ruling: τρυφᾶν means live luxuriously/feast, not just rejoice; contrast with κολάζει requires stronger rendering.

edits.old: so virtue makes those who work at it rejoice even before the kingdom.
edits.new: so virtue makes those who work at it feast in delight even before the kingdom.

fixed: Changed 'rejoice' to 'feast in delight' to reflect τρυφᾶν (live in luxury/delight).

last_rejected.quote: Do not be zealous about faith, beloved, yet more sluggish about zeal itself
last_rejected.source_quote: Μὴ ἴσθι, ἀγαπητέ, περὶ μὲν τὴν πίστιν σπουδαῖος, περὶ δὲ τὴν σπουδὴν ὀκνηρότερος
last_rejected.why: σπουδή means 'diligence/effort', not 'zeal itself'; the contrast is faith vs. diligence/effort in practice, not zeal about zeal.
last_rejected.fix: Do not be zealous about faith, beloved, yet more sluggish about diligence
last_rejected.ruling: σπουδή can mean 'zeal' or 'diligence'; 'zeal itself' captures the wordplay with σπουδαῖος/σπουδή acceptably.

last_rejected.why: ἀφιλόσοφος means 'not loving wisdom/untrained in philosophy', i.e., neglectful of moral wisdom; 'unphilosophical' is too modern/technical.
last_rejected.ruling: ἀφιλόσοφος literally means 'unphilosophical'; within normal range for moral context, not a major error.
